blocks.x: This is John Steiner. I'm interviewing Bob Lovett, a clarinetist who admired and played in the New Orleans style in the 1948-49 period when he was a student at the University of Chicago. Bob was friendly with many of the New Orleans men who were around town and because of his intimate acquaintance with them, I thought that an interview might shed some light from the standpoint of a practicing musician who was not actually from New Orleans but who enjoyed the New Orleans influence and knew he did. We're interviewing this evening. This is April 28, 1964. The people in that group, Bob Lovett, will tell you about. The voice hereafter will be that of Bob Lovett's, except where I may at times offer interjection or question.

Bob, when did you start playing clarinet? Probably when I was about 16, maybe 15 years old. That would have been around 1940 or 41. Where were you at the time? At that time I was in Boston, Massachusetts. Do you remember what influenced you to be interested in the clarinet? Yes, I was interested in jazz at that time. I had bought quite a few records. I had heard some Louis Armstrong records. In those days I wasn't very discriminating in my taste and I just sort of liked jazz in general.
Was there anything about the clarinet that also attracted you?
Actually, I played trombone before I played clarinet. But for some reason or other I couldn't seem to get with the trombone. I switched after a few months to clarinet. I don't remember exactly why.
Were you given instruction?
Yes, I took some lessons from time to time with different legitimate clarinet teachers.
Did you take lessons on trombone?
Yes, I had taken some.
This was all legitimate in spite of your jazz interest. You hadn't tried to get lessons in jazz immediately.
Oh no, no. But I experimented playing jazz from as soon as I started playing the clarinet at all.
Were some of the prominent clarinet men more or less your idols in those days? Goodman or Shaw?
I'm trying to think.
Barney, Bigard, Pee Wee?
I think probably the first clarinetist I was impressed by was Pee Wee Russell.
Did you hear Pee Wee in Boston? No, not at that age.

Yeah, as a matter of fact I did. I heard him at a place called, it was called the Ken Club. This was during the war. And Bill Davison came to town with a band with Pee Wee and Brad Gowans and James P. Johnson and Kaiser Marshall. It was quite a band. He was also a guitar player. That's right, Jack Goss. Yeah, I remember. I wish I could hear that band again.

Well, strangely enough, Bill wrote to me from Boston and said, this is the best band I ever had, you ought to record us. At that time I was interested in records. And I knew the small chances I'd have of getting Bill to record the band himself. But I wrote back and said, is there a good studio in Boston and do you want to record a couple sides? Let me hear what they're like. And he said, yes, for $10 we can go in for an hour. So I sent him the $10. Of course nothing ever happened. I didn't hear the band. But they came to Chicago without James P. Johnson. Maybe without Brad. And I heard them then. And it was an excellent band. Now, you were, this was at the age of what? Well, maybe 15, 16 years old, I guess. So?
They used to have Sunday afternoon sessions at that place in which if you were a minor you could come in, they didn't serve drinks. It was just a...

And you'd heard enough music so that at that age you were getting a little excited about music. Yeah, yeah. Did you have any other artistic bent? Did you have the idea you might go into artistic enterprise as you grew older?
I didn't really know what I wanted to do at this age, but the idea of being a jazz musician sort of appealed to me romantically. Unfortunately it did for too many years.
I was a little bit of a jazz musician. I was a little bit of a jazz musician. I was a little bit of a jazz musician.

No, I wasn't good enough then. I was just learning. We had a little group, I remember, in Boston, a few fellows I know, including Dan Gerald, who you know, who I was in prep school with. There was a trumpet player and piano player and Dan Gerald on drums and myself. How does Gerald spell his name? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And we used to play at the trumpet player's house. His name was Ted Fales. And I began to become more under New Orleans influence. I began to listen to the Hot Fives, Jelly Roll Morton, King Oliver, and that sort of thing. And we sort of tried to emulate that. Were the other fellows similarly impressed? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes, I think so. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Was it Dan who aroused that interest or all of you spontaneously? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I can't remember exactly, but we used to play records and talk about them and we decided that that was the best form of jazz. That's what we should try to do. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Do you remember any tunes that you used? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Oh. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Oh. We played many of the jazz standards, the jazz me blues and...

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Any records stand out in your mind? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. You mean that I heard? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Do you recall of that period? Yes, that you'd imitate for example. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Oh, yeah. Some of the...

Some of the Hot Five records I think we used as models. I can't remember exactly which ones. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Did you depend on written scores to get an idea of how the chords went? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No. At that period, most of us were sort of unfamiliar with what chords were. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And we just faked it. I mean, you know, we played entirely by ear and did the best we could. And I guess we had a lot of fun, but most of it sounded awful.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Now you mentioned Jolly Roll and Louie. Do you remember any of the other recording leaders?
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, some of those small groups were Johnny Dodds. Generally the New Orleans groups we were mainly impressed with.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. By that time they had become also called the South Side groups. They had made many of these recordings in Chicago. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. They were the New Orleans men. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Now, many of the early Chicagoans had listened to the original Dixieland Jazz Band, then later to the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. At any time do you remember those coming into your observation?

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes, the New Orleans Rhythm Kings I remember we listened to. And yes, I remember I was impressed by Rapolo. I liked him. In fact, I remember I used to play his solo on the Tin Roof Blues, and I was very proud of the fact that I could play that.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Was there an effort to emulate his tone and effects as well as just the phrase?
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No, I think I was mainly trying to emulate the sound of Johnny Dodds.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Even that early or after the Dodds? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I think so, yes. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Because? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Because to me it seemed like a good, strong, gutsy sort of thing. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. As you recall, I mentioned that later in a chapter in New Perspectives of Jazz, where your playing in the Dodds style had impressed me so that years later I remembered it. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. How did you have to come to Chicago?

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, I came to the University of Chicago after I got out of the Navy. I got out of the Navy in 1946. And my friend Dan Gerald, who I had played with in Boston and who we had a mutual interest in jazz, he was at the University of Chicago. So I came here under the G.I. Bill of Rights. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. What did you take up at the University? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I took the liberal arts course in the college. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Still thinking of being a musician, possibly? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Oh yes, I was very much interested in that. I wanted to get an education, but I think I was mainly interested in becoming a musician.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Was Gerald behind the formation of the jazz group at Chipoga?

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, Dan was playing with what members of it were here then. He was here a year or so before I came here. And after I came here, he sort of became interested in other things. And Jack Selden became the drummer.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Jack Selden was from Texas, is that right? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And I remember him going back and I corresponded with him years later, but I hadn't heard of him in recent years. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. That is maybe in mid-50s or something. I don't know if we had an exchange or two. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Now in 49, you came to, 48 rather, you came to the University. And do you remember who made up the first groups that you played with? Was it then called the Cakewalking Babies?

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, it didn't have a name at first. We just sort of thought that was a hot sounding name, so we adopted it. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. It was Bill Price on trumpet and Alan Fredrickson on trombone and myself. And there was a piano player named Paul Jackson and a banjo player named Paul Boeberg and Jack Seldon on drums. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And I think that was the regular group. There may have been others who played from time to time.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Then about the time you left, some of the others left too, that is the band more or less broke up about 50, didn't it? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Bill Price kept a group together, but your group had pretty well spread.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah, right.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. As a group, did you do any professional work? Do you remember any jobs that you got paid for?

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah, I think we played a few jobs. I can't, I think we played some fraternity house jobs at the university and things like that. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I remember we played a concert at Mandel Hall. I think it was a benefit for the United Negro College Fund. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And Art Hodes was there, and Baby Dodds, and Preston Jackson, myself and Bill Price. And I think that was it.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Do you happen to recall where Baby Dodds might have heard of the band? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I think that's where he heard me the first time. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. There's a report in one of the French magazines about Baby saying, oh, there's somebody who plays like my brother in Chicago now, you needn't worry about the next generation.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Oh really? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Do you remember Baby saying anything like that to you? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes, I remember he said something very flattering to me about that.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I don't remember exactly what he said. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, your style was distinctly more like Johnny Dodds, I think, than I've ever heard anyone else attain. And this was a definite effort on your part. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Oh yeah,
that was a conscious effort. And I wasn't trying to be original at all. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, that was a little early, perhaps. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah. G-E-R-O-U-L-D.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, I'm not going to dwell on originality. I can understand how you might pick some mentor and stay with him. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. But that was after Johnny had died, wasn't it? You never met Johnny?
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No, I never met him or I never saw him or heard him in person. I guess he died when?

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. In the early 40s, I think. I can't remember. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And what you know about Johnny what you know about Johnny, then you took off of records, except maybe what you read. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. But your style derived from what you would hear on records. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes, entirely. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Any of the other boys in that group make an effort to emulate the New Orleans men? Now I'm talking about the University of Chicago group.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, I think Bill Price did. Bill Price was very much influenced by Louis and Bunk and possibly some of the others like George Mitchell.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Bill Price now lives in Minneapolis, but frequently comes to Chicago and he hears about a jam session where he might sit in. So he comes down sometimes for a Sunday session where there is advertised there will be ten bands. Well, he knows that if he comes down there enough people know him that he'd get in one of those bands. So he's on and on for a set or two. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And I understand that he works occasionally in Minneapolis, becoming a friend of Doc Evans and other...

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I saw Bill a few months ago in New York at a benefit at the Central Plaza for Jack Crystal. In fact, I saw just about everybody in the world there. It's one of those things everybody turned up.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Did he go to New York for that or happened to be in New York?
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No, he just happened to be in New York in business or something. I don't... I've forgotten.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Have you heard about any of the other people besides Bill from your cakewalking babies
continuing their interest in... G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No, I have no idea what's happened to any of the others.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. You say that Art Hody sat in with you. If I remember, Don Ewell used to occasionally.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah, Don used to play with us quite often. In fact, I think we may have made some records which have become lost.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, we'll try to find them. We talked about the styles that you were emulating. It seems to me that the trombone might also.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah, well, I'd say he was probably vaguely influenced by King Ori and Jim Robinson. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. But I don't think he was... I don't think he listened to jazz that closely. I mean, I don't...
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, now that I think of it, you might also say it may be Jimmy Archie, because it's a puffing kind of performance that might even be more Archie than Ori.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I remember we played some sessions at Jimmy Yancey's house. And people like Cripple Clarence Lofton would come in. I remember that. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And you played with him? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. With Jimmy. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. You remember ever playing with Lofton? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I don't think I ever actually played with him, but I was there one night when he came in and sat down and played.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Just lately I've written a note about Lofton saying that because it was difficult for people to play with him, not many say that they sat in with Lofton. Even drummers found it a little difficult. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Since he was a soloist and so much an individualist. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. But no problem playing with Jimmy Yancey, of course. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No, no.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Played the standard blues. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes, he liked us very much, I remember.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. You don't remember recording with Jimmy Yancey? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No, I don't think we did. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Were there other New Orleans people you know? Now you mentioned at the concert, Preston Jackson, did you ever work with him again? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No, I think that was the only time I ever saw him or played with him. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And Baby Dodds, do you remember working with him elsewhere?
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I don't actually remember working with him anywhere else.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, I mentioned, yes, I mentioned that I had heard you with Baby Dodds, I'm quite certain about this, G-E-R-O-U-L-D. In a park on the edge of Lake Michigan at about 55th Street. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I think it was called Promontory Park or something of that sort. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And it was a field house or a band house or something of that sort out there in the park. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. On a weekend night, probably a Friday night, playing for a dance and some of the jazz enthusiasts at the school may have promoted it. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I don't remember the circumstances for it. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. But I would suspect that it was Cakewalking Babes with Baby Dodds either setting in for a set or maybe for a while. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Did Bill Russell ever run a session out there? Is it possible that it was Bill Russell's session?

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I don't think so. I remember I met Bill Russell once when I was with Don Ewell. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Bill Russell came to town for something or other. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I remember I met him once.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, Bill wasn't living here at that time then. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, alright. Then he wouldn't have run. Later on when he came into town he began to run some sessions.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Oh, I do remember later I played with Baby Dodds at the Central Plaza in New York, possibly in 1950 or 51. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Was Bunk too? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No. No, this was after Bunk left.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And then I started a question, but I guess I laid you off a little bit. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Were there other New Orleans men that you remember having played with around Chicago? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Well, Lee Collins. Did we mention him? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. No, we haven't. And you said that you have a photograph of your band with Lee Collins.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes, I have with Bill Price and all those fellas playing with Lee Collins at the Victory Club, which was on North Clark Street. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. We used to go down there quite a lot.
G-E-R-O-U-L-D. It seemed to me that if anybody could sit in, there weren't many restrictions. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. That's right, yeah. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. So, Lee had what? Three, four pieces?

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. It was himself and there was a piano player named Sweet William, I believe. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Actually, I think his name was William Sweet. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Oh, oh. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah, but everybody used to call him Sweet. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And I don't know if he had a regular drummer there or not.

G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Freddie Flynn? Do you remember that? G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yes, I remember the name. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Freddie Flynn, frequently drummed for him. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. All right, I'd like to stop this for a moment. . . . . Thank you.
. The End

If the tape which I intend to prepare were played continuously, your performance of April 1949 with the Cakewalking Babes, which was recorded at the Myron Bachman studio on Carmen Avenue, just off Broadway about 5200 north, would have been heard, and we'll go back to a discussion of the Victory Club. Do you remember other people at the Victory Club besides your group, and these we've named, do you ever run into anybody else there?
Yeah, there were people who used to drop in and play. I'm trying to think of...
Paul Merez had a place for a little while in the neighborhood. Do you ever see him?
No, I think that was gone when I came to Chicago.
Was Brunus and Tony Peretti around? They used to go in. Tony Peretti did, I don't remember having seen Brunus at the Victory Club.
No, as a matter of fact, I think Brunus was in New York at that period with Bill Davison and Condon. Oh yes. I think Brunus...
It may be a little later than the period I'm thinking of.
No, I can't remember the names of anybody else that came in.
Do you see any of the Chicago fellas there? There were... The piano players, Tut Soaker and Mel Grant around. Do you have to run into those while you were in Chicago? Yes, yes.
I saw them. Places like the Beehive and... I don't know, different places around. I remember, yeah, Tut Soaker and Mel Grant. I remember Mel Grant playing with Doc Evans.
And I never saw them at the Victory Club. No, they weren't generally. That was such a horrible piano, you can understand.
Oh yeah, sure. Half the keys were missing.

They wouldn't be. There was a little fellow played trumpet, played it badly, but tried very hard to imitate Louis by the name of Louis Zachera. Did you ever see Louis Zachera at the Victory Club? I remember him. Year after year, he'd be a frequent visitor. I don't remember the name. Louis Zachera once had a job running a freight elevator. And somebody said, Louis, I understand you're the best freight elevator in the world. And Louis looked at him and said, you know, I'd rather be the worst trumpet player than the best freight elevator in the world. And I think he made it. Yeah. Do you remember any other spots? You mentioned Victory Club and Beehive. Yeah. Any other places you'd stop in? Is the Blue Note alive at that time? No. I think that was before the Blue Note. Well, it was Jazz Limited.
I used to go there quite a lot because I knew people who were working there like Don Yule and Dick Wells did. I used to like to hear Sidney Bechet who was working there for a while.
Did you at any time show a tendency to follow Bechet or were you strictly on a Dodds game?

No, actually I didn't really like Bechet that much. I liked Dodds much better. And I went through a period later where I thought Bechet was terrible and absolutely unlistenable. And now I sort of come back to him. I like a good deal of his work. I think he's a great musician. You told me that you took lessons after you arrived in Chicago, right? No, I never took any lessons while I was in Chicago. How did you get along with school work and your interest in music? Did they match up? No, I'm afraid the school work suffered. That's why I only stayed there a year. And I never finished college. I was still possessed by this dream of becoming a jazz musician. And I think I had some illusions in those days that what I was doing was more important than it really was. In those days, I used to think that if you could play the same notes that Johnny Dodds did and if you played the same tunes, that you were doing the same thing. And of course it's not that easy.
Did you get any idea about sitting out and playing your own notes and being more an individualist?

No, I don't think so. I was always a very imitative musician. Later I got away from the New Orleans influence and I came back to Pee Wee Russell. I don't know if you're aware of this, but when I went to New York, this was mainly due to the influence of Mark Groves. And I began to become more interested in Pee Wee Russell, that understated form of playing rather than the extroverted New Orleans style. And then I went for many years imitating Pee Wee instead of imitating Johnny Don. And for a while I was playing very much like Frank Chase plays. I guess not as well, but it was that sort of thing.

It seems to me Marty told me that you had changed your approach. Yes. This was after Marty had been in Chicago, went back to New York and heard you there and came back and said that you enjoyed what you were doing. You seemed to be reasonably happy. There wasn't enough work, maybe that was the problem.

Yeah. Yeah. Who did you work with? I worked, for about a year and a half I made a living working with Conrad Janis. Who was, he started out as a Kid Ori imitator. And I guess he's still doing it. He still has those sessions at the Central Plaza. But he was never, I don't think he was ever really seriously interested in playing any kind of jazz. I mean, he's an actor, that's his main profession and that's sort of his approach to music is that he's a showman and he'll do anything to please the crowd. I mean, he stands up there and jumps up and down and sweats and his hair falls down. He's sort of the Elvis Presley of the trombone. And the New Orleans influence is just sort of incidental. And I played with him for a while. And this was after I was out of the New Orleans Circle of influence. What year was that? Oh, I guess that was about 50 or 51, 52. Soon after returning. Yeah. How did you have to go back to New York? Uh, well, I just felt a need to get out of Chicago for a number of reasons. I hadn't done well at school and I felt I was sort of floundering around here and I thought there might be more opportunities as a musician in New York. And, uh, uh, uh, the piano player that I knew Dick Wellstead, who, uh, who incidentally is another very much New Orleans influenced musician. Although he's also, uh, I guess he's more influenced by the Harlem pianists, James P. Johnson and, uh, dear Yes, I think at some of those sessions at the Central Plaza I worked quite a lot with Danny Barker. He was a New Orleans man. And there were others too. I can't...
You said Baby Downs was in New York.
Baby Downs was there for a while. I think he had a stroke at that time. And he wasn't too active.
I'm trying to think. Was Simeon around at that time? Did he start to play at Ryan's?

I don't remember Simeon being around then, no. But he came in later with Wilbur de Paris. Pops Foster? Pops Foster was there, yes. Yes. I remember I played with Pops Foster. In fact, I went with Wellstead up to Pops Foster's house. He was a delightful man. Very charming host.
Did you meet Barney Bigard? No. I thought in connection with your clarinet. I ran into him. Zooty.
Zooty. Yes. I've worked with Zooty at the Central Plaza. I remember that now.
Was Peretti in New York at that time?
Yeah, Peretti was around. I remember seeing him a lot.
Because he and Wellstead worked a lot later. Yes. Right. Did Janice have any steady jobs in this period that you were with him?

Yes. Mostly at the Central Plaza. We used to work there every Friday and Saturday night. And we used to work a few other jobs too. We did, I don't know, we were on the Arthur Godfrey Show. A lot of things like that. Who else was in the band? A guy named Dick Smith on trumpet. He was from the west coast. He was influenced by Bunk mainly. And, well, before I was in the band, there was a clarinet player named Tom Sharpstein, who used to do a very good imitation of George Lewis. And, when I was in the band, the piano player was Elmer Schoble. You know who he is. Yes, indeed.

And, he certainly was pleased with the first New Orleans men to come up because he worked with them steadily. Both at the Friars and at Midway Gardens. Although, now that I say Midway, I can't remember that there were many New Orleans. They were mainly Chicagoans. However, they were greatly influenced by the Friars where Schoble had been active. Did Schoble continue his activity in composing or arranging at that time?
Yes, I think he was trying to sell some tunes. And, I don't think he got very far with it. But, he wasn't very active otherwise.

I can't remember that there were any New Orleans pianists around New York with a possible exception. Lou Russell was out of the band business by that time. Yeah, Lou Russell died about six months ago. And, uh... No, offhand, I can't remember who the others who might have been around New York. But, if you don't recall of mine, it's not likely that we missed many of the first generation men.
No, I don't think so.
What influenced you to reconsider music as a livelihood? Because it wasn't a livelihood?

Partially because it wasn't a livelihood and also it just wasn't very satisfying aesthetically, having to play with a lot of bad musicians for bad audiences who just wanted to hear a lot of noise. Partially because it wasn't a livelihood. And, gradually I became aware of the fact that I really wasn't doing anything that justified devoting your life to it.

You didn't get a creative satisfaction out of it? That's right. I just became aware that I was just doing a second-rate imitation of first-rate musicians that I couldn't hope to come close to. Did you get to record it all in New York? There wasn't anything there, was there? Are you on any of the Janus records?
Not on any of the records that were issued, no. But, there are some air shots that we did that I've heard tapes of. I don't have them myself.
I don't have them, no. And, did an opportunity come along that knocked you out of music or did you just drop music?

No, I just sort of gradually got away from it. After I left Janus and I had various day time jobs, I was still working once in a while as a clarinet player on weekends. But, I began to do less and less of it. And, gradually I just got away from it entirely. I became too much involved in other things.
When did you get into movie work?
Around 1955.
And, did you start out as an editor, movie editor?
Yes, I started out editing newsreels in a television station in Philadelphia. I went down there for a year.
And, how did that happen to lead into your presence, actually?

Well, I decided there were more opportunities for film editors in New York. And, I came back to New York and I got a job for a producer of industrial films. I did that for a few years, commercials and things like that. And, now I work on feature films.
In the editing, are you called upon to make decisions yourself on what will be included in the...
Yes, constantly you're making decisions. Small ones, but it's the sum of many small decisions that build the picture.
Who do you work most closely with in this? The producer?
The director. The director. Yes. I guess the director. Yes. In fact, the editing is actually an extension of the work that the director does.
So, do you spend a lot of your time editing at his side?

Well, I mean, he doesn't actually spend a great deal of time in the cutting room. I mean, he doesn't stand over your shoulder and tell you where to cut, but he looks at the work you've done every day or every couple of days or maybe once a week, depending on a lot of things. And, he will make suggestions and tell you what he thinks is wrong with the sequence and ask you to rework it and look for... Try to emphasize certain aspects of the scene and de-emphasize others. It's a process of trial and error.
You say that you haven't been playing for a long time, right?
No, I haven't actually touched the clarinet for a couple of years now.
Well, did it have something to do with being busy or being satisfied or not having work?

Well, I would like... I think sometimes that I would like to play and you pick up the clarinet and your fingers don't move as fast as they used to and your lip gets tired and so you get discouraged and you put it away and you don't touch it again for a long time. And so every time you pick it up it works, so eventually you just stop altogether. Too fresh, isn't it? Yes, yeah. That's one of those things you have to keep at it constantly or else you lose touch with it.

Well, so many people who drop out of music find an opportunity to play once in a while and decide that they, oh, we'll forget the loss of technique forgetfulness of tunes and so forth. Yeah. Well, you just go ahead and try. Yeah. And I know that they feel somewhat disappointed with their performance. Yeah. Others are so disappointed and I think that maybe they were a little tense in their original endeavors. that they were so devoted that they can't stand that disappointment. George Mitchell is one of those. Oh. George has refused for 20 years to play publicly. Yeah. Yet, when I called on him the last time his music rack was up. Oh, yeah. As if he'd been reading. So, so. But he refused to play. How old is he now? I'd guess in the 70s. Mm-hmm. Franz Jackson invited him to play when Bob Schaffner was ill. Mm-hmm. And, well, maybe he would. But he says maybe I think instead of saying no. Yeah. Yeah. He means no. Because he has it. And, uh, uh, there are several who, uh, can't get over the fact that they are losing touch with their peak performance and they can't count on doing less than their best.
Right. Yeah, it is a distressing thing.
Do you enjoy listening, uh, as, we won't say as much, that's hard to gauge, but do you enjoy listening as you did years ago?

Oh, yes. Every, every bit as much. I, I still, you know, buy records as reissues and things that come out, you know. Mm-hmm. I, I listen as much as I ever did and I guess I maybe appreciate a lot of things that I didn't used to.
In other words, you feel that, knowledgeably, you're farther ahead with every year. Mm-hmm.

Yeah. Yeah, I love jazz as much as I ever did. Still, uh, in a, a New Orleans groove? Uh, yes. Well, I, my tastes have broadened. I mean, uh, I went through a period, you know, first I would like nothing except authentic New Orleans jazz and, and then I broke away from that and I wanted nothing except, uh, authentic, if there is such a thing, authentic Chicago style jazz. And now my tastes are broad enough that I can listen to both and get something from it. Mm-hmm.
Uh, do you go, uh, uh, uh, do you cover a broader span? Do you listen to Ellington or do you listen to...
Oh, yes, yes. Yes, Ellington and, uh, you know, I like all kinds of things. I collect tapes of the Mills Blue Rhythm Orchestra and all.
Mainly, uh, instrumental. Uh, yes, but some vocal stuff.

I, you know, I like Bessie Smith and, uh, I even like, uh, a lot of folk artists, uh, you know, uh, jazz, basically jazz folk artists like Lightning Hopkins. Uh, I like Lead Belly and, uh, Leroy Carr and a lot of, a lot of people like that, you know. A lot of things I didn't used to listen to that I got a great deal of pleasure from now.

I think we've covered a pretty good segment of your, uh, experience and your attitude toward music and we've come to the end of the tape. Good. We don't have to strain you any further. You see, it really isn't an easy job to run for an hour and you can imagine the problems that some of these interviewers have had when they've interviewed people for days at a time. Sometimes it's possible. I haven't had an experience myself because an hour is a good long run.

segments.title: Interviewer's introduction of Bob Lovett
segments.summary: Steiner introduces Lovett, a clarinetist in the New Orleans style at the University of Chicago in 1948-49, and gives the interview date.

segments.title: Starting clarinet in Boston, after trombone
segments.summary: Lovett began clarinet at 15-16 after a few months of trombone, took legitimate lessons, and improvised jazz from the start.

segments.title: Pee Wee Russell and the Davison band at the Ken Club
segments.summary: Pee Wee Russell was his first clarinet idol; he heard Bill Davison's band with Russell at a Boston club, and Steiner recalls trying to record it.

segments.title: Boston prep-school group with Dan Gerould, imitating Hot Fives
segments.summary: With Dan Gerould and friends he played by ear, modelling on Armstrong, Morton and Oliver records.

segments.title: New Orleans Rhythm Kings, Rappolo and modelling on Johnny Dodds
segments.summary: He learned Rappolo's Tin Roof Blues solo but mainly tried to emulate Johnny Dodds's strong, gutsy sound.

segments.chapter: University of Chicago and the Cakewalking Babies
segments.title: University of Chicago and the Cakewalking Babies
segments.summary: After the Navy he came to Chicago on the GI Bill; Steiner and he list the Cakewalking Babies' members.

segments.chapter: University of Chicago and the Cakewalking Babies
segments.title: Paid jobs, Mandel Hall concert, and Baby Dodds on Lovett's Dodds style
segments.summary: The band played fraternity jobs and a Mandel Hall benefit with Art Hodes, Baby Dodds and Preston Jackson; Dodds praised his Johnny Dodds-like style.

segments.chapter: University of Chicago and the Cakewalking Babies
segments.title: Bill Price, band members' fates, Don Ewell sitting in
segments.summary: They discuss Bill Price's later life, lost track of other members, and Don Ewell sitting in and possible lost recordings.

segments.title: Sessions at Jimmy Yancey's house, Cripple Clarence Lofton, Preston Jackson
segments.summary: Lovett recalls sessions at Yancey's house where Lofton played, and says he played with Preston Jackson and Baby Dodds only at the concert.

segments.title: Baby Dodds at a lakefront dance, Bill Russell, later gig in New York
segments.summary: Steiner recalls hearing the band with Baby Dodds at a park dance; Lovett met Bill Russell once and later played with Dodds in New York.

segments.title: Playing with Lee Collins at the Victory Club
segments.summary: Lovett's band sat in with Lee Collins at the Victory Club on North Clark Street, where Sweet William and Freddie Flynn played.

segments.title: Tape change
segments.summary: A garbled tape-end passage.

segments.title: Other musicians at the Victory Club and Chicago pianists
segments.summary: After the tape resumes, they recall who visited the Victory Club, Chicago pianists, and trumpeter Louis Zachera.

segments.title: Jazz Limited, Sidney Bechet, and school work suffering
segments.summary: He frequented Jazz Limited, preferred Dodds to Bechet, and his schoolwork suffered so he left after a year.

segments.title: Turning from Dodds to Pee Wee Russell in New York
segments.summary: He was always imitative; in New York he shifted to Pee Wee Russell's understated style under Marty Grosz's influence.

segments.title: Working with Conrad Janis and why he moved to New York
segments.summary: He earned a living about 18 months with Conrad Janis, whom he describes as a showman, and moved to New York seeking more opportunities.

segments.title: New York musicians: Baby Dodds, Pops Foster, Zutty, Parenti
segments.summary: They ask who was around New York: Baby Dodds after a stroke, Pops Foster, Zutty Singleton and Tony Parenti.

segments.title: The Janis band: Central Plaza, personnel, and Elmer Schoebel
segments.summary: Janis's band played Fridays and Saturdays at the Central Plaza and on Arthur Godfrey, with Dick Smith, Tom Sharpstein and Elmer Schoebel.

segments.title: Giving up music as a livelihood
segments.summary: He left because it was unprofitable and aesthetically unsatisfying, and faded away from music after leaving Janis.

segments.title: Becoming a film editor
segments.summary: He started editing newsreels in Philadelphia, moved to New York industrial films and features, and describes working with directors.

segments.title: Not touching the clarinet; musicians who stop playing
segments.summary: He hasn't played in years; they discuss loss of technique and George Mitchell refusing to play.

segments.title: Listening tastes broadened beyond New Orleans
segments.summary: He enjoys listening as much as ever, now appreciates New Orleans, Chicago, Ellington, blues and folk artists.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Steiner ends the tape with comments on interview length.
